transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-02
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Mark Liu (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Anika Shah (Redwood), James Patel (Helios), Sara Gomez (Helios), Tom Chen (Helios), Lina Park (Helios)

Summary (auto): SE walkthrough of Dedicated vs Hosted perf characteristics with focus on isolation/noisy neighbor, KV cache strategies, and quantization impacts. Agreed on benchmark plan and next steps.

Topics: runtime perf, p95 latency, throughput guarantees, capacity fencing, KV/prefix cache, batching, quantization, VPC/offline deployment, audit logs

Transcript:
[00:00] Mark Liu: All right, welcome everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Mark from Redwood, AE on the account. Today's goal is to map perf expectations and architecture choices for dedicated capacity versus our hosted tier.
[00:22] James Patel: Yep thanks Mark, we have called this because last week we saw a couple of spikes in our routing, and we want to validate isolation strategies. Our SRE Lina is here and she'll speak to tail latency.
[00:35] Priya Nair: Hi, Priya, Redwood SE. I'll lead the technical side — we'll go over KV cache, batching, quantizaton tradeoffs and then sketch a benchmarking plan. Note, apologies if audio cuts — my son's in the background.
[00:50] Sara Gomez: Hi all, Sara. I'm most interested in throughput, token costs, and how caching affects hallucination risk — will caching change model outputs for us?
[01:05] Tom Chen: Tom here — security checklist: VPC peering, KMS keys, audit logs, and whether on-prem option is feasible for our compliance needs.
[01:18] Mark Liu: Good. Quick agenda: 1) perf numbers for Dedicated vs Hosted, 2) isolation/noisy neighbor mitigation, 3) KV cache design and TTLs, 4) batching and quantization, 5) open Q&A and next steps.
[01:32] Priya Nair: Kicking off with runtime: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools — we can guarantee instance level isolation and predictable batching windows. For single-stream p95 latency we measured ~80-110ms on A100-like hardware with a 2k token context for GPT-like models under continuous batching disabled. Hosted can hit similar medians but p95 varies during multi-tenant bursts — noisy neighor spikes.
[02:05] James Patel: When you say noisy neighbor spikes, what's magnitude? 200ms, 400ms?
[02:12] Priya Nair: We've seen p95 jump to ~300-600ms in high contention on hosted multi-tenant when a tenant floods with long seqs, depending on scheduling and kernel availability. Dedicated essentially flattens that — you'll still see variance from seq lengths but not from other tenants.
[02:30] Lina Park: That's significant. Our SLO is 95th under 120ms for interactive features. Dedicated sounds closer but what's the throughput cost?
[02:41] Priya Nair: There's a cost tradeoff. Dedicated lets you tune batch windows and pre-warm KV caches. You can get higher sustained throughput because you can pack continuous batching more aggressively without cross-tenant fairness constraints. For example, in our internal bench, dedicated pools achieved 2.0–2.6k tokens/sec per GPU for medium sequence workloads with quantized weights, whereas hosted averaged 1.2–1.8k under mixed noisy workloads. These are workload dependent.
[03:10] James Patel: Can you explain the KV cache topology — local KV vs shared prefix cache?
[03:18] Priya Nair: Sure. Two common patterns: 1) Local KV per instance for low-latency prefix hits (fastest, less sharing), 2) Shared prefix layer at the edge or redis-like store for warm prefixes across requests — trades write/read latency for hit-rate. We sometimes do hybrid: hot prefixes sticky to instances, mid-tier shared cache. Note transcription: sometimes we see K V spelled out in logs — sorry.
[03:47] Sara Gomez: How does TTL affect correctness? If we cache tokens, could outputs diverge?
[03:53] Priya Nair: Caching only KV for decoder state preserves determinism for the same prompt. But prefix caching of embeddings or partial prompts can introduce stale context if your prompt templates change. TTLs should be aligned with your prompt mutation frequency. We recommend short TTLs (30s–5min) for rapid prompt churn, longer (30m–hours) for stable system prompts.
[04:18] Mark Liu: On quantization — Anika, want to summarize?
[04:22] Anika Shah: Yes — quantizaton to int8 or int4 saves memory and increases throughput but impacts per-token quality slightly. We did AB tests: int8 had negligible quality delta for retrieval-augmented prompts, int4 showed measurable hallucination increases on low-temp sampling. For determinism, quantization can change logits subtly; we recommend running eval sets.
[04:47] Tom Chen: For compliance, if we go Dedicated in a VPC, do you support customer KMS? HSM?
[04:54] Priya Nair: Yes Dedicated + Private supports customer-managed KMS keys and HSM integrations. For on-prem we can plug into enterprise KMS but there is an ops integration effort. We'll include checklist.
[05:09] [06:15] — (cross talk, audio artifact)
[05:20] James Patel: Does caching change the attack surface? If someone gets access to shared cache could they infer other customers' prefixes?
[05:28] Priya Nair: Good question. Shared caches must be tenant-scoped or encrypted at rest; we typically shard by tenant or use namespacing. For highly regulated customers we suggest Dedicated with local instance caches only to minimize shared state.
[05:42] Mark Liu: Let's talk about autoscaling and capacity fencing: Dedicated supports reserved capacity + burst lanes. If traffic spikes beyond reserved, we have fallback policies to route to hosted variants, with controlled cost and latency impact.
[05:59] Lina Park: So fallback means if dedicated pool is saturated, requests go to hosted and p95 increases? How do we prevent degraded user experience?
[06:07] Priya Nair: You can set SLO-aware fallback rules — e.g., only overflow non-critical routes or degrade gracefully for background jobs. We can also configure canary scale-ups, and prewarming policies.
[06:24] Sara Gomez: On batching — continuous batching is good for throughput but increases single-request latency because you wait for batch fill. How does Redwood balance this?
[06:33] Priya Nair: We have adaptive batching: short tail latency requests get prioritized with tighter batch windows; background batches aggregate. There's also prefix-aware batching to avoid cross-stream interference when KV states differ.
[06:46] James Patel: Could you quantify the latency tradeoff? If we enable batching for throughput, what's the extra ms per request?
[06:53] Priya Nair: Typical batching windows are 5–20ms; but with waiting for batch completeness you might add 10–60ms in exchange for 2x–5x throughput depending on sequence lengths. The per-token kernel execution is more efficient in batches.
[07:10] Tom Chen: Any recommended settings for our interactive mode vs batch mode?
[07:14] Priya Nair: Interactive: small batch window (<=10ms), prioritize single-streams, local KV. For high throughput async jobs: larger windows (20–50ms), quantization allowed, shared caches with warm-up. We'll produce a config template.
[07:28] Mark Liu: On noisy neighbor detection — we expose tracing and token-level cost breakdowns in Redwood Console. We can show which tenant caused long-running kernels. That helps if you want to petition capacity or a kernel fix.
[07:41] Lina Park: Is there a way to cap per-tenant concurrency inside Dedicated to avoid one internal service spiking?
[07:47] Priya Nair: Yes, we support per-tenant concurrency caps and enforcement at routing layer. Dedicated also allows pool partitioning — soft fences within a reserved pool. Hard fencing is more expensive (dedicated instances per workload).
[08:02] Sara Gomez: You mentioned bench numbers earlier — can you share real sample runs with our model shape? Our models are ~4B with 2k context and 1–2 token completions mostly.
[08:12] Priya Nair: We'll run a bench with your token distribution. For 4B models with int8 quant, dedicated got ~1.8–2.2k tok/sec/GPU in our internal tests with 2k contexts. Hosted multi-tenant showed 0.9–1.4k under mixed load. We'll share raw logs and configs.
[08:30] James Patel: About benchmarking — what metrics should we provide? P50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, memory headroom, kernel queue depth?
[08:38] Mark Liu: Exactly. Also include arrival distribution, average request size, percent of single-turn vs multi-turn, and failure rates. We'll set up a shared spreadsheet.
[08:46] [09:00] (audio skip)
[09:12] Priya Nair: On quantization one more note: mixed precision kernels can give near-float performance while keeping some layers in fp16 to preserve accuracy. For critical routes, we recommend mixed precision over aggressive int4.
[09:28] Tom Chen: For private deployments, how do you handle audit logs and data residency?
[09:32] Priya Nair: Private mode supports customer-controlled log retention in their VPC and explicit audit logging with S3/Elasticsearch endpoints you own. We support region pinning and can mirror logs to your SIEM.
[09:46] James Patel: If we run on-prem, will we still get Redwood Console visibility?
[09:50] Mark Liu: Yes via a private control plane. You can opt-in to telemetry; otherwise, we run a console instance in your VPC with RBAC and SSO.
[10:01] Sara Gomez: Let's discuss cache warm-up. Cold starts cause higher latency — what's the typical warm-up strategy?
[10:08] Priya Nair: We do proactive warm-up during deploys: pre-populate KV for expected prefixes, run synthetic traffic to fill caches, and maintain a small warm pool. For new models we recommend a warm-up window during rollout.
[10:20] Lina Park: Any tips on measuring noisy neighbor impact in hosted before committing to Dedicated?
[10:26] Priya Nair: Yes — we can run a hosted stress test with synthetic tenants to reproduce contention. Also Redwood Console traces let you correlate high p95 with tenant kernel spans. We'll run a hosted stress bench and compare to a dedicated replica.
[10:40] Mark Liu: Pricing note: Dedicated has a base monthly commit but predictable per-token costs. Hosted is pay-as-you-go with variable tails. We'll send an apples-to-apples cost model.
[10:53] James Patel: About fallback — if we overflow to hosted, can we control which model variant is used? For example, fallback to smaller quantized model rather than same model on hosted?
[11:01] Priya Nair: Yes, routing policies can map to model variants. You can route overflow to quantized smaller variants to retain latency but accept quality tradeoff. That's a common strategy.
[11:14] Sara Gomez: Any known quality regressions when moving from fp16 dedicated kernels to quantized hosted variants?
[11:20] Anika Shah: Usually you'll see small shifts in token probabilities. On eval sets this can reduce BLEU-like scores slightly; for retrieval-augmented tasks it's often imperceptible. We'll include evaluation diffs.
[11:33] [12:00] (laughter, unrelated)
[11:40] Tom Chen: From security: we need to see SOC2 and penetration test reports before rooftop approval.
[11:46] Mark Liu: We'll share SOC2 and the last pentest summary. For private deployments, we can arrange a security workshop.
[11:54] Priya Nair: Back to batching: prefix-aware batching reduces cross-request KV thrash by grouping requests with similar cache state. This reduces cache misses by ~15–30% on some workloads.
[12:10] James Patel: If our UI requires sub-100ms p95, is Dedicated the only route?
[12:16] Priya Nair: Not necessarily. With careful batching config, prewarmed caches, and small batch windows, Hosted can meet sub-100ms for moderate loads. But at peak multi-tenant contention Dedicated is much more reliable.
[12:30] Lina Park: Ok, that helps. Next, what's required from our infra team to run a pilot?
[12:36] Mark Liu: We need a sample traffic dump, SLOs, IP allowlist for VPC peering, and security contact for the questionnaire. We'll also ask for model artifacts (if private) and storage access for cache layers.
[12:47] Sara Gomez: We'll provide sample traces and the SLO doc. Also, what's the expected timeline for a two-week pilot?
[12:53] Priya Nair: Typical pilot: 1 week of setup/warm-up, 1 week of ramped load + analysis. We can start benchmarks within 3 business days after we get artifacts.
[13:05] James Patel: Does Redwood support kernel-level tuning if we hit a bottleneck?
[13:10] Priya Nair: Yes our runtime team can iterate on kernel choices and compile-length specific kernels — but that's a deeper engineering engagement. We'll log tickets as needed.
[13:22] Mark Liu: Any other big concerns?
[13:25] Tom Chen: One more: data deletion and customer keys — need SLA for key rotation and deletion.
[13:30] Priya Nair: We'll include KMS lifecycle and deletion SLAs in the security pack.
[13:37] [13:50] (brief pause)
[13:55] Mark Liu: Quick recap of agreed actions: Redwood will share bench results for Dedicated and Hosted with your model shape, KV cache diagram, and config templates. Helios will share traffic histograms, SLOs, and security questionnaire. Pilot kickoff tentatively week of 2025-09-15.
[14:15] James Patel: That sounds good. Can we also see a cost simulation of fallback scenarios?
[14:20] Mark Liu: Yes we'll include overflow cost scenarios and model variant routing examples.
[14:27] Priya Nair: I'll also attach a short note on quantization best practices and an eval checklist for your QA team.
[14:35] Sara Gomez: Thanks everyone — looking forward to the bench runs.
[14:40] Mark Liu: Great, thanks all. We'll follow up with links in an email.
[14:45] (Meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional word swaps (K V, quantizaton, noisy neighor), filler words and brief audio artifacts present.
